items.prompt: Explain how providing bread can satisfy customers and support the bakery’s survival. Omuti Foods is a small bakery supplying bread to families in a Namibian town. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Business activity organises resources to provide goods or services that satisfy wants and needs. A need is something essential for living, while a want is a particular way someone would like a need or desire satisfied. Producing something is not sufficient for commercial success: the offer must reach customers at a price and quality they accept. A private enterprise normally seeks enough revenue to cover costs and provide a return; other organisations may prioritise a service or social objective. The bakery combines ingredients, equipment and people to make bread available locally. Customers obtain food without baking it themselves, while sales give the bakery revenue with which to pay its costs. Revenue is not the same as profit: costs must be deducted. A shortage of customers or rising costs can prevent an otherwise useful business from surviving.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Business activity organises resources to provide goods or services that satisfy wants and needs.

items.prompt: Explain how the bakery can respond to the needs of its community. Families near Omuti Foods need bread before the early bus leaves, and the bakery has an unused early shift. [6]
items.canonical_answer: A community includes customers, workers, nearby residents and other organisations. Businesses can respond by supplying needed goods and services, creating work, purchasing from local suppliers and supporting useful local projects. A response is stronger when the business first identifies a specific need rather than assuming that everyone wants the same thing. Community benefit and business benefit may coincide, but a useful service can still be costly to provide. Opening earlier could make breakfast purchases more convenient and increase sales if enough families use the service. Hiring local workers can bring household income into the area. The bakery must compare the extra demand with wages, electricity and transport costs: a community response is more sustainable when it can be maintained without exhausting the business’s resources.

items.prompt: Distinguish primary, manufacturing and trading activities by what happens to the product and who buys it. A fishing operation lands fish; a processor freezes packaged portions; a shop sells them to families. [6]
items.canonical_answer: To distinguish activities, follow what happens to the resource or product and who receives the output. Extraction differs from transformation; selling to another business differs from selling to the final consumer. A service can support a physical product without itself being manufacturing. These distinctions prevent classifying an enterprise solely from its size, its name or the fact that it earns money. The fishing operation obtains a natural resource, while the processor transforms or prepares it for sale. The shop’s transaction with a family is retailing. A firm buying cartons from the processor and reselling them to shops performs wholesaling. The ownership form could be the same at several stages without changing the activity performed.
marking_guidance: Difference: To distinguish activities, follow what happens to the resource or product and who receives the output.

items.prompt: Explain how public services and economic policy can affect a small bakery. In a policy example, a road improvement shortens Omuti Foods’ delivery route while borrowing becomes more expensive. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Government can provide services and infrastructure, regulate business activity, raise revenue and influence economic conditions. Public services may support business by improving skills, transport or health. Regulation can address harms that private decisions impose on others. Fiscal policy concerns government spending and taxation; monetary policy concerns monetary and credit conditions, including interest rates. The tools differ, and their effects depend on the situation rather than being guaranteed. The road can reduce delivery delays and transport expense, helping the bakery reach customers. A higher borrowing cost can make a new oven less affordable, so expansion may be postponed. Government expenditure on the road is a fiscal action; the change in credit conditions belongs to monetary policy. Calling both tools taxation would hide the different mechanisms.

items.prompt: Distinguish market, planned and mixed systems in their decision making and possible consequences. A town has privately owned bakeries and publicly provided roads and schools. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Economic systems concern how resources are allocated and how production decisions are made. In a market model, private decisions and prices have a major coordinating role. In a planned model, central public decisions direct a substantial part of production and allocation. A mixed economy combines private enterprise with public ownership, provision and regulation. These are models: actual economies differ in the extent and form of intervention. The town illustrates a mixed arrangement: private producers decide what bread to offer, while public provision supports the community. Market competition may encourage responsiveness and cost control, but people with little purchasing power may not obtain all the services they need. Planning can pursue collective priorities, but planners may lack detailed local information. A comparison should connect a feature to its consequence rather than label one system good in every situation.
marking_guidance: Difference: Economic systems concern how resources are allocated and how production decisions are made.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether dividing the bakery’s work into specialised tasks is suitable. Omuti Foods has steady orders for standard loaves but is considering accepting many individually decorated celebration breads. [8]
items.canonical_answer: Specialisation can improve skill through repetition, reduce time spent changing tasks and allow equipment to be used intensively. These gains may raise output or reduce unit costs if the stages are coordinated and demand supports the output. Limitations include repetitive work, dependence on other stages and a loss of flexibility. A specialised skill or product may become less useful when demand changes. Skills for cover can be developed through on-the-job or off-the-job training; the choice of training method is explained in Topic 3.5, while the point here is continuity between specialised tasks. A task-based line suits repeated standard loaves because workers can practise a narrow activity and organise batches efficiently. It may be less suitable when orders differ substantially or one absent worker stops a stage. A sensible judgement is to specialise the repeated standard work while retaining flexible skills for varied orders. If most demand becomes individual orders, that balance should change.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Specialisation can improve skill through repetition, reduce time spent changing tasks and allow equipment to be used intensively.

items.prompt: Explain how specialising in bread increases the bakery’s need for trade. Omuti Foods specialises in bread and purchases flour and repair services from other local suppliers. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Trade is the buying and selling or exchange of goods and services. Specialisation and trade support each other: concentrating on some activities leaves other needs to be met through exchange, while access to a wider market can make specialisation worthwhile. Selling output can provide the income needed to buy inputs or other products. Trade still depends on reliable supply, demand and acceptable terms. The bakery does not need to grow grain and repair every machine itself. It can sell bread and use revenue to buy those inputs and services. This allows attention to be focused on baking, but creates dependence on suppliers. If flour deliveries become unreliable, the benefits of concentration may be reduced. Trade is the exchange linking specialised activities; it is not another name for the specialisation itself.

items.prompt: Explain why higher wages may conflict with customer and owner objectives. Workers at Omuti Foods request higher pay while customers resist a price rise and the owners need to maintain cash for repairs. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Objectives conflict when pursuing one makes another harder to achieve. Conflict can occur between groups or within one group’s priorities. Raising wages can reduce short-term profit if other conditions are unchanged; reducing prices may help customers but leave less money to cover costs. A conflict is not proof that cooperation is impossible: changes in productivity or a negotiated compromise may help several groups. Paying more without extra revenue increases costs and can reduce the funds available for repairs. Passing the full increase to customers may reduce sales. A phased wage change combined with feasible waste reduction could ease the conflict, but the savings must be achievable. The explanation must connect each objective to a constraint rather than merely list that groups want different things.

items.prompt:
Nawa Rolls is a bakery in Otjiwarongo. It sells standard rolls to shops, buys flour from a mill and uses separate workers for mixing, shaping and baking. Orders are steady, but an absent oven operator can delay output.

(a)(i) Define specialisation. [2]
(a)(ii) State two transactions that link this specialised bakery to other businesses. [2]
(b) State two tasks that could be allocated to different bakery workers. [2]
(c) Explain one benefit and one limitation of division of labour for Nawa Rolls. [6]
(d) Evaluate whether Nawa Rolls should retain narrow specialised tasks. [8]
items.canonical_answer: (a)(i) Concentrating on a particular product, activity or skill. Here the firm concentrates on baking. (a)(ii) Buying flour from the mill and selling rolls to shops are two trade transactions. (b) Mixing dough and operating the oven are distinct tasks. (c) Repetition can improve skill in shaping standard rolls, reducing avoidable mistakes if workers are trained. However, dependence on the oven operator can leave other stages waiting when that person is absent. (d) Retaining some specialised tasks suits steady standard orders, where repeated work can be organised efficiently. The absence problem means the bakery should also cross-train a worker to cover the oven. If training and cover are feasible, a coordinated division of labour is preferable to making each worker complete every stage; if reliable cover is impossible, broader roles may protect continuity. Specialisation still requires trade for flour and outlets for finished rolls.

items.prompt:
Nawa Rolls is a bakery in Otjiwarongo. It sells standard rolls to shops, buys flour from a mill and uses separate workers for mixing, shaping and baking. Orders are steady, but an absent oven operator can delay output.

(a) Explain how specialisation creates both a need for trade and dependence on other businesses at Nawa Rolls. [8]
(b) Evaluate whether the benefits of division of labour outweigh its limitations for the bakery. [12]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Concentrating on rolls means the bakery buys flour rather than growing and milling grain itself. A dependable mill allows attention to be focused on baking, but interrupted supply can stop output. Selling to shops gives access to customers without the bakery performing every retail transaction; dependence on those shops’ orders means a lost outlet can reduce demand. Division of labour also links the internal stages, so coordination is needed as well as external trade. (b) Repeated standard orders favour specialised tasks: workers can develop skill and arrange work efficiently. Against that, the absent oven operator exposes a vulnerable stage and repeated work may reduce interest. Trade allows access to inputs and markets but does not remove those internal risks. Retaining the system with feasible cross-training and coordinated scheduling is a reasoned choice because it keeps the repetition benefit while addressing the specific disruption. If orders become varied or cover cannot be organised, flexibility becomes more valuable and the judgement should change.

items.prompt:
Etango Bakes is a small bakery serving cafés. Most orders are standard rolls. It buys flour and packaging from other businesses and is considering dividing its work into narrower tasks.

Evaluate whether Etango Bakes should introduce narrower specialised tasks. Present a decision plan using specialisation, trade and the dependence between production stages. [12]
items.canonical_answer: Knowledge: specialisation concentrates activity; division of labour divides production tasks; trade exchanges output and inputs. Application: standard café orders give repeated tasks, while flour and packaging come from other firms. Analysis: repetition may improve speed and skill, but late inputs or a stalled stage can interrupt output. Alternative: broader worker roles offer flexibility but involve more switching and a wider range of skills. Judgement: introduce a limited division of labour where the repeated work is sufficient, with planned cover and reliable suppliers. A narrow task should not be adopted merely because it looks efficient if it creates an uncovered bottleneck.

items.prompt:
Etango Bakes is a small bakery serving cafés. Most orders are standard rolls. It buys flour and packaging from other businesses and is considering dividing its work into narrower tasks. For part (b), the stated constraint changes: most customers now order small quantities of individually shaped celebration breads rather than standard rolls.

(a) Evaluate the suitability of division of labour for Etango Bakes under its original order pattern. [12]
(b) Evaluate whether your decision should change under the new celebration-bread order pattern. [12]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Standard rolls allow mixing, shaping and baking to be organised as repeated stages. This may build skill and save switching time, provided the stages match demand and one does not constrain the rest. The bakery still needs trade for flour and packaging and outlets for its rolls. A narrow system creates dependence and can be repetitive, so it should be combined with feasible cover rather than an assumption that every worker must remain at one task. A coordinated division of labour is suitable for the original stable pattern. (b) Individually shaped orders create greater variety and smaller runs. Broader skills now help workers respond to different specifications, so the earlier degree of specialisation may be too rigid. Some repeated preparation can remain specialised, but flexible roles around shaping and finishing become more useful. The trade links remain necessary; what changes is the internal balance between repetition and flexibility. This conditional change is stronger than claiming that division of labour is either suitable or unsuitable for every bakery.
